study.title: Study of Proverbs 13
study.overview: Proverbs 13 gathers short sayings that contrast wisdom and folly in very practical areas: speech, discipline, work, relationships, money, hope, correction and moral character. The chapter shows that godly life is not only a matter of knowledge, but of willingness to listen, learn, control the language, receive rebuke and walk with wise people. It also teaches that lasting results usually accompany justice, while sin, arrogance and lack of judgment produce shame, need, and ruin.

outline.title: Listen correction, keep speech and deal with the heart
outline.explanation: The first sayings deal with the wise son who accepts discipline, the value of words, the dominion of language, diligent work and inner falsehood. The chapter begins by showing that wisdom appears in the willingness to learn and in the way a person speaks and acts.

outline.title: Wealth, conflict and hope
outline.explanation: This section contrasts the value and danger of riches, the arrogance that generates quarrels, the lengthy hope that weakens the heart and the fulfilled desire that renews the soul. The focus is on the effect of attitudes of the heart on conviviality and perseverance.

outline.title: Word, commandment, competition, and practical wisdom
outline.explanation: Here are themes such as respect for good education, the teaching of the sage as a source of life, the common sense that gains favor and the effect of friendships. The text insists that rejecting correction brings losses, while walking with wise wisdom.

outline.title: Moral Retribution, Inheritance and Discipline of Children
outline.explanation: The final verses claim that evil perseses sinners and that the righteous receive good, deal with inheritance, economic prudence, correction of children and the sufficiency of the righteous in contrast to the need of the wicked. The closure unites justice, discipline and contentment.

study.context: Proverbs 13 is part of a collection of sapiential sayings attributed to Solomon in a broad sense in the book of Proverbs. The chapter presents general observations on moral and social life, without narrating a specific history. Its scenario is the daily life of the family, work, the use of the word, social relations and the education of children.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that biblical wisdom is practical and moral: listening to correction, mastering the language, avoiding pride, welcoming teaching and cultivating godly friendships are part of a straight life before God. Justice is not presented as an abstract ideal, but as a path that preserves, honor and leads to true satisfaction. At the same time, the text shows that sin disorders desires, corrupts speech, weakens hope and produces need. There is also a strong emphasis on discipline as an expression of love and the responsibility to form character from an early age. In an evangelical perspective, this harmonizes with the idea that God forms his people through instruction, correction and wisdom received with humility, without transforming these attitudes into self-autonomous human merit.

scholarViews.insight: The control of the tongue is presented as a sign of wisdom; keeping the mouth protects life and soul.
The righteous is described as a satisfied and moderate person in their desires, while the wicked remains insatiable and in need.
The pride is seen as a cause of contention; humility would be the opposite way, capable of promoting peace and restoration.

questions: How does my reaction to correction reveal whether I'm teachable or scoffer?
Has my speech preserved the lives of others and mine, or has it spread recklessness and conflict?
Are my friendships making me wiser or more foolish?
study.practice: Practise three concrete attitudes today: listen to a rebuke without defending yourself immediately; choose words that build and avoid impulsive comments; and get closer to a wise person to ask for advice in a real area of life. Also examine if your work routine, finance and family discipline expresses God's contentment, responsibility and fear.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are limited and, in some points, summarize the sense of verses without developing their full range. There is not enough base in the notes to identify specific historical details, nor to state with certainty the authorship of each individual proverb. Commentators' readings should be received as interpretations, not as final definitions of the text.
